claim: Phase-amplitude coupling between theta and multiple gamma sub-bands is a hallmark of hippocampal activity.
source: Phase-amplitude coupling between theta and multiple gamma sub-bands is a hallmark of hippocampal activity and believed to take part in information routing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about hippocampal activity patterns.

claim: Phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma is believed to take part in information routing.
source: Phase-amplitude coupling between theta and multiple gamma sub-bands is a hallmark of hippocampal activity and believed to take part in information routing.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical interpretation supported by the scientific community.

claim: Theta and gamma oscillations were reported to exhibit phase-phase coupling or n:m phase-locking.
source: More recently, theta and gamma oscillations were also reported to exhibit phase-phase coupling, or n:m phase-locking, suggesting an important mechanism of neuronal coding that has long received theoretical support.
evidence: This claim references prior reports in the literature about phase-phase coupling.

claim: n:m phase-locking has long received theoretical support as an important mechanism of neuronal coding.
source: More recently, theta and gamma oscillations were also reported to exhibit phase-phase coupling, or n:m phase-locking, suggesting an important mechanism of neuronal coding that has long received theoretical support.
evidence: This references theoretical work supporting phase-locking as a coding mechanism.

claim: Quasi-linear phase shifts introduced by filtering lead to spurious coupling levels in both white noise and hippocampal LFPs.
source: We show that the quasi-linear phase shifts introduced by filtering lead to spurious coupling levels in both white noise and hippocampal LFPs, which highly depend on epoch length, and that significant coupling may be falsely detected when employing improper surrogate methods.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by simulations and data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spurious coupling levels highly depend on epoch length.
source: We show that the quasi-linear phase shifts introduced by filtering lead to spurious coupling levels in both white noise and hippocampal LFPs, which highly depend on epoch length, and that significant coupling may be falsely detected when employing improper surrogate methods.
evidence: This finding is demonstrated through analysis of different epoch lengths shown in Figure 2C and Figure 5B.

claim: Significant coupling may be falsely detected when employing improper surrogate methods.
source: We show that the quasi-linear phase shifts introduced by filtering lead to spurious coupling levels in both white noise and hippocampal LFPs, which highly depend on epoch length, and that significant coupling may be falsely detected when employing improper surrogate methods.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of different surrogate methods in Figure 2F and Figure 5B.

claim: Waveform asymmetry may generate artifactual n:m phase-locking.
source: We also show that waveform asymmetry and frequency harmonics may generate artifactual n:m phase-locking.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of sawtooth waves in Figure 4.

claim: Frequency harmonics may generate artifactual n:m phase-locking.
source: We also show that waveform asymmetry and frequency harmonics may generate artifactual n:m phase-locking.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of harmonic frequencies in Figure 4 and Figure 7.

claim: Cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma oscillations has been well described in the hippocampus.
source: Cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma oscillations has been well described in the hippocampus, whereby the instantaneous amplitude of gamma oscillations depends on the instantaneous phase of theta (Scheffer-Teixeira et al., 2012; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The instantaneous amplitude of gamma oscillations depends on the instantaneous phase of theta in the hippocampus.
source: Cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling between theta and gamma oscillations has been well described in the hippocampus, whereby the instantaneous amplitude of gamma oscillations depends on the instantaneous phase of theta (Scheffer-Teixeira et al., 2012; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Hippocampal theta and gamma oscillations were reported to exhibit n:m phase-phase coupling in which multiple gamma cycles are consistently entrained within one cycle of theta.
source: More recently, hippocampal theta and gamma oscillations were also reported to exhibit n:m phase-phase coupling, in which multiple gamma cycles are consistently entrained within one cycle of theta (Belluscio et al., 2012; Zheng and Zhang, 2013; Xu et al., 2013, 2015; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This references multiple prior studies reporting phase-phase coupling.

claim: The existence of different types of cross-frequency coupling suggests that the brain may use different coding strategies to transfer multiplexed information.
source: The existence of different types of cross-frequency coupling suggests that the brain may use different coding strategies to transfer multiplexed information.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the existence of multiple coupling types.

claim: Coherent oscillations are believed to take part in network communication by allowing opportunity windows for the exchange of information.
source: Coherent oscillations are believed to take part in network communication by allowing opportunity windows for the exchange of information (Varela et al., 2001; Fries, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Standard phase coherence has been associated with cognitive processes such as decision-making.
source: Standard phase coherence measures the constancy of the phase difference between two oscillations of the same frequency (Lachaux et al., 1999; Hurtado et al., 2004), and has been associated with cognitive processes such as decision-making (DeCoteau et al., 2007; Montgomery and Buzsáki, 2007; Nácher et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cross-frequency phase-phase coupling has previously been hypothesized to take part in memory processes.
source: Cross-frequency phase-phase coupling has previously been hypothesized to take part in memory processes (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Jensen and Lisman, 2005; Lisman, 2005; Schack and Weiss, 2005; Sauseng et al., 2008, 2009; Holz et al., 2010; Fell and Axmacher, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: The Rn:m metric successfully detects n:m phase-locking in coupled Kuramoto oscillators.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, the coupled – but not uncoupled – oscillators exhibited a prominent peak for n:m = 1:5, which shows that Rn:m successfully detects n:m phase-locking.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: When Kuramoto oscillators are coupled, the mean frequencies align to a 1:5 factor by changing from 8 Hz and 43 Hz to 8.5 Hz and 42.5 Hz, respectively.
source: When coupled, the mean frequencies aligned to a 1:5 factor by changing to 8.5 Hz and 42.5 Hz, respectively (see Guevara and Glass, 1982; García-Alvarez et al., 2008; Canavier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation with theoretical support from citations.

claim: Filtered white-noise signals exhibit a bump in the Rn:m curve at the ratio of the analyzed frequency ranges.
source: For each frequency pair, we constructed n:m phase-locking curves for epochs of 1 and 10 s, with n = 1 fixed and m varying from 1 to 25 (Figure 2B). In each case, phase-phase coupling was high within the ratio of the analyzed frequency ranges: Rn:m peaked at m = 4–6 for θ−γS, at m = 7–11 for θ−γM, and at m = 12–20 for θ−γF.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of white noise shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The existence of a bump in the Rn:m curve may merely reflect the ratio of the filtered bands and should not be considered as evidence for cross-frequency phase-phase coupling.
source: Therefore, the existence of a 'bump' in the Rn:m curve may merely reflect the ratio of the filtered bands and should not be considered as evidence for cross-frequency phase-phase coupling: even filtered white-noise signals exhibit such a pattern.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the white noise analysis results.

claim: The bump in the Rn:m curve of filtered white noise is explained by the fact that neighboring data points are not independent.
source: The bump in the Rn:m curve of filtered white noise is explained by the fact that neighboring data points are not independent.
evidence: This explanation is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phase shift between two consecutive data points follows a probability distribution highly concentrated around 2*π*fc*dt, where fc is the filter center frequency and dt the sampling period.
source: In fact, the phase shift between two consecutive data points follows a probability distribution highly concentrated around 2*π*fc*dt, where fc is the filter center frequency and dt the sampling period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: No Rn:m bump occurs when data points of the gamma phase time series are made independent by sub-sampling with a period longer than a gamma cycle.
source: In accordance to this explanation, no Rn:m bump occurs when data points of the gamma phase time series are made independent by sub-sampling with a period longer than a gamma cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), or when extracting phase values from different trials (not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of filtering-induced sinusoidality on Rn:m values is stronger for narrower frequency bands.
source: As expected, the effect of filtering-induced sinusoidality on Rn:m values is stronger for narrower frequency bands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For any fixed n:m ratio and frequency pair, Rn:m decreased as a function of epoch length.
source: In fact, for any fixed n:m ratio and frequency pair, Rn:m decreased as a function of epoch length (see Figure 2C for θ−γS and R1:5): the longer the white-noise epoch the more the phase difference distribution becomes uniform.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phase-phase coupling has positive bias for shorter epochs.
source: In other words, as standard phase coherence (Vinck et al., 2010) and phase-amplitude coupling (Tort et al., 2010), phase-phase coupling has positive bias for shorter epochs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and compared to known properties of other coupling metrics.

claim: False-positive coupling may be detected if control (surrogate) epochs are longer than the original epoch.
source: As a corollary, notice that false-positive coupling may be detected if control (surrogate) epochs are longer than the original epoch.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the epoch length dependence of Rn:m.

claim: Rn:m computed from a pool of surrogate runs is much smaller than when computed for each individual run.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2E, Rn:m computed from a pool of surrogate runs is much smaller than when computed for each individual run.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2E.

claim: Pooling instantaneous phase differences across 10 runs of 1 s surrogate epochs is equivalent to analyzing a single surrogate epoch of 10 s.
source: This is due to the dependence of Rn:m on the epoch length: pooling instantaneous phase differences across 10 runs of 1 s surrogate epochs is equivalent to analyzing a single surrogate epoch of 10 s.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical properties of the Rn:m metric.

claim: θ−γS phase-phase coupling in white noise was statistically significantly larger than in phase-scrambled surrogates.
source: However, as shown in Figure 2F for θ−γS as an illustrative case (similar results hold for any frequency pair), θ−γS phase-phase coupling in white noise was statistically significantly larger than in phase-scrambled surrogates (for either Single Run or Pooled distributions).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Original Rn:m values were not statistically different from chance distributions when these were constructed from Single Run Rn:m values for either Time Shift and Random Permutation surrogate procedures.
source: On the other hand, Original Rn:m values were not statistically different from chance distributions when these were constructed from Single Run Rn:m values for either Time Shift and Random Permutation surrogate procedures (Figure 2F; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neither scrambling phases nor pooling individual surrogate epochs should be employed for statistically evaluating n:m phase-locking.
source: We conclude that neither scrambling phases nor pooling individual surrogate epochs should be employed for statistically evaluating n:m phase-locking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the surrogate analysis results.

claim: Chance distributions should be derived from surrogate epochs of the same length as the original epoch and which preserve phase continuity.
source: Chance distributions should be derived from surrogate epochs of the same length as the original epoch and which preserve phase continuity.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the analysis results.

claim: Original R1:5 values were much greater than the surrogate distribution for coupled but not uncoupled Kuramoto oscillators.
source: Original R1:5 values were much greater than the surrogate distribution for coupled – but not uncoupled – oscillators (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Variability in the instantaneous frequency leads to low n:m phase-locking levels for independent oscillators even when their mean frequencies are perfect integer multiples.
source: This result illustrates that variability in the instantaneous frequency leads to low n:m phase-locking levels for independent oscillators even when their mean frequencies are perfect integer multiples.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results in Figure 3A.

claim: Coupled oscillators have high Rn:m because variations of their instantaneous frequencies are mutually dependent.
source: On the other hand, coupled oscillators have high Rn:m because variations of their instantaneous frequencies are mutually dependent.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The model LFP exhibited significant n:m phase-locking only when the interneurons were coupled.
source: Compared to Single Run surrogate distributions, the model LFP exhibited significant n:m phase-locking only when the interneurons were coupled; Rn:m levels did not differ from the surrogate distribution for the uncoupled network (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: High asymmetry of the theta waveform may lead to statistically significant Rn:m values per se.
source: However, it should be noted that high asymmetry of the theta waveform may also lead to statistically significant Rn:m values per se.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of sawtooth waves in Figure 4.

claim: A non-sinusoidal oscillation such as a theta sawtooth wave can be decomposed into a sum of sine waves at the fundamental and harmonic frequencies.
source: As illustrated in Figure 4A, a non-sinusoidal oscillation such as a theta sawtooth wave can be decomposed into a sum of sine waves at the fundamental and harmonic frequencies, which have decreasing amplitude (i.e., the higher the harmonic frequency, the lower the amplitude).
evidence: This is a known property of Fourier decomposition illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The harmonic frequency components are n:m phase-locked to each other.
source: Importantly, the harmonic frequency components are n:m phase-locked to each other: the first harmonic exhibits a fixed 1:2 phase relationship to the fundamental frequency, the second harmonic a 1:3 relationship, and so on (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Higher frequency harmonics exhibit cross-frequency phase-phase coupling to the fundamental theta frequency.
source: Of note, the higher frequency harmonics not only exhibit cross-frequency phase-phase coupling to the fundamental theta frequency but also phase-amplitude coupling, since they have higher amplitude at the theta phases where the sharp deflection occurs (Figure 4C left and Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see also Kramer et al., 2008 and Tort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with support from citations.

claim: Higher frequency harmonics exhibit phase-amplitude coupling to the fundamental theta frequency.
source: Of note, the higher frequency harmonics not only exhibit cross-frequency phase-phase coupling to the fundamental theta frequency but also phase-amplitude coupling, since they have higher amplitude at the theta phases where the sharp deflection occurs (Figure 4C left and Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see also Kramer et al., 2008 and Tort et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with support from citations.

claim: The gamma-filtered component of a theta sawtooth wave of variable peak frequency displays spurious gamma oscillations that have a consistent phase relationship to the theta cycle irrespective of variations in cycle length.
source: The gamma-filtered component of a theta sawtooth wave of variable peak frequency thus displays spurious gamma oscillations (i.e., theta harmonics) that have a consistent phase relationship to the theta cycle irrespective of variations in cycle length.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of sawtooth waves in Figure 4C.

claim: The spurious n:m phase-coupling induced by sharp signal deflections is significantly higher than the Random Permutation/Single Run surrogate distribution.
source: As a result, the spurious n:m phase-coupling induced by sharp signal deflections is significantly higher than the Random Permutation/Single Run surrogate distribution (Figure 4C right and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 top row).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The significance of spurious coupling from sharp deflections is much lower when using the Time Shift procedure compared to Random Permutation.
source: Interestingly, the significance of this spurious effect is much lower when using the Time Shift procedure (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 bottom row), probably due to the proximity between the original and the time-shifted time series (200 ms maximum distance).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Rn:m curves of hippocampal LFPs peaked at n:m ratios according to the filtered bands.
source: Namely, Rn:m curves peaked at n:m ratios according to the filtered bands, and Rn:m values were lower for longer epochs (Figure 5A; compare with Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of hippocampal LFPs shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Rn:m values of hippocampal LFPs were lower for longer epochs.
source: Namely, Rn:m curves peaked at n:m ratios according to the filtered bands, and Rn:m values were lower for longer epochs (Figure 5A; compare with Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Original Rn:m values of hippocampal LFPs were not statistically different from a proper surrogate distribution (Random Permutation/Single Run) in epochs of up to 100 s.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, Original Rn:m values were not statistically different from a proper surrogate distribution (Random Permutation/Single Run) in epochs of up to 100 s (but see Figure 10).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: False positive phase-phase coupling would be inferred if an inadequate surrogate method (Time Shift/Pooled) were employed on hippocampal LFPs.
source: Noteworthy, as with white-noise data (Figure 2F), false positive phase-phase coupling would be inferred if an inadequate surrogate method were employed (Time Shift/Pooled) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Phase-phase plots of actual LFPs displayed diagonal stripes.
source: However, as in previous reports (Belluscio et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2016), phase-phase plots (2D histograms of theta phase vs gamma phase) of actual LFPs displayed diagonal stripes (Figure 6), which seem to suggest phase-phase coupling.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and referenced to prior reports.

claim: The LFP exhibited spectral peaks at harmonic frequencies due to the non-sinusoidal shape of theta.
source: Due to the non-sinusoidal shape of theta (Belluscio et al., 2012; Sheremet et al., 2016), the LFP also exhibited spectral peaks at harmonic frequencies (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7A with support from citations.

claim: The number of diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots was determined by the harmonic order.
source: Similarly to the sawtooth wave (Figure 4B), the phase-phase plots exhibited diagonal stripes whose number was determined by the harmonic order (i.e., the 1st harmonic exhibited two stripes, the second harmonic three stripes, the third, four stripes and the fourth, five stripes; Figure 7Bi–iv).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both gamma and 35 Hz filtered signals exhibited the exact same phase lag in phase-phase plots.
source: Interestingly, when the LFP was filtered at a broad gamma band (30–90 Hz), we observed five diagonal stripes, the same number as when narrowly filtering at 35 Hz; moreover, both gamma and 35 Hz filtered signals exhibited the exact same phase lag (Figure 7Biv–v).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots may be influenced by theta harmonics.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that the diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots may be influenced by theta harmonics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis in Figure 7.

claim: Signals filtered at the gamma band would be likely to exhibit as many stripes as expected for the first theta harmonic falling within the filtered band.
source: Under this interpretation, signals filtered at the gamma band would be likely to exhibit as many stripes as expected for the first theta harmonic falling within the filtered band.
evidence: This is an inference based on the harmonic analysis.

claim: The peak frequency of theta relates to the number of stripes in phase-phase plots.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found that the peak frequency of theta relates to the number of stripes (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Phase-phase plots constructed using data averaged from individual time-shifted epochs exhibited no diagonal stripes.
source: As in previous studies (Belluscio et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2016), phase-phase plots constructed using data averaged from individual time-shifted epochs exhibited no diagonal stripes (Figure 7Bvi and Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7Bvi and Figure 8, with reference to prior studies.

claim: Different time shifts lead to different phase lags, causing diagonal stripes of individual surrogate runs to cancel each other out when combining data across multiple runs.
source: This is because different time shifts lead to different phase lags; the diagonal stripes of individual surrogate runs that could otherwise be apparent cancel each other out when combining data across multiple runs of different lags (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phase-phase plots constructed from filtered white-noise signals displayed diagonal stripes.
source: As shown in Figure 9A, phase-phase plots constructed from filtered white-noise signals also displayed diagonal stripes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 9A.

claim: The sinusoidality induced by the filter can by itself lead to diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots.
source: Since white noise has no harmonics, these results show that the sinusoidality induced by the filter can by itself lead to diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots, in the same way that it leads to a bump in the Rn:m curve (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the white noise analysis.

claim: Bin counts in phase-phase plots of white-noise signals were deemed statistically significant when compared to the distribution of bin counts from time-shifted surrogates.
source: Importantly, as in actual LFPs, bin counts in phase-phase plots of white-noise signals were also deemed statistically significant when compared to the distribution of bin counts from time-shifted surrogates (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 9A.

claim: The statistical analysis of phase-phase plots as originally introduced in Belluscio et al. (2012) is too liberal.
source: Since by definition white noise has no n:m phase-locking, we concluded that the statistical analysis of phase-phase plots as originally introduced in Belluscio et al. (2012) is too liberal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the white noise analysis results.

claim: Phase-phase plots of white noise were no longer statistically significant when using the Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
source: Nevertheless, we found that phase-phase plots of white noise were no longer statistically significant when using the same approach as in Belluscio et al. (2012) but corrected for multiple comparisons (i.e., the number of bins) by the Holm-Bonferroni method (the FDR correction still led to significant bins; not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated through statistical analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: For all epoch lengths, Original Rn:m values of white noise fell inside the distribution of Single Run surrogate Rn:m values computed using either Time Shift and Random Permutation procedures.
source: Consistently, for all epoch lengths, Original Rn:m values fell inside the distribution of Single Run surrogate Rn:m values computed using either Time Shift and Random Permutation procedures (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 9B.

claim: The presence of diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots is not sufficient to conclude the existence of phase-phase coupling.
source: Here we showed that the presence of diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots is not sufficient to conclude the existence of phase-phase coupling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of white noise and actual LFPs.

claim: For epochs of up to 100 s, bin counts in phase-phase plots of actual LFPs were no longer statistically significant after correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: For epochs of up to 100 s, we found similar results as in white noise, namely, bin counts were no longer statistically significant after correcting for multiple comparisons (Holm-Bonferroni method); this was true when using either the Time Shift or Random Permutation procedures (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 10A.

claim: When analyzing much longer time series (10 or 20 min of concatenated periods of REM sleep), several bin counts became statistically significant when compared to randomly permutated, but not time-shifted, surrogates.
source: Surprisingly, however, when analyzing much longer time series (10 or 20 min of concatenated periods of REM sleep), several bin counts became statistically significant when compared to randomly permutated, but not time-shifted, surrogates (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 10A.

claim: The Original Rn:m curve of actual LFPs fell within the distribution of Time Shift/Single Run surrogate Rn:m values for all analyzed lengths.
source: Moreover, this result reflected in the Rn:m curves: the Original Rn:m curve fell within the distribution of Time Shift/Single Run surrogate Rn:m values for all analyzed lengths, but outside the distribution of Random Permutation/Single Run surrogates for the longer time series (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 10B.

claim: The very low coupling level (~0.03) observed in long LFP epochs is unlikely to have any physiological significance.
source: But if this is the case, we consider unlikely that the very low coupling level (~0.03) would have any physiological significance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots of both white noise and actual LFPs are mainly caused by a temporary n:m alignment of the phase time-series secondary to the filtering-induced sinusoidality.
source: We conclude that the diagonal stripes in phase-phase plots of both white noise and actual LFPs are mainly caused by a temporary n:m alignment of the phase time-series secondary to the filtering-induced sinusoidality, and as such they are also apparent in surrogate data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of white noise and actual LFPs.

claim: For actual LFPs there is a second influence on diagonal stripes, which can only be detected when analyzing very long epoch lengths, and which is believed to be due to theta harmonics.
source: However, for actual LFPs there is a second influence, which can only be detected when analyzing very long epoch lengths, and which we believe is due to theta harmonics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of long LFP epochs.

claim: There is lack of convincing evidence for n:m phase-locking in the hippocampal LFPs analyzed in this study.
source: Since Original Rn:m values were not greater than Single Run surrogate distributions, we concluded that there is lack of convincing evidence for n:m phase-locking in the hippocampal LFPs analyzed here.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the data analysis.

claim: Previous work may have spuriously detected phase-phase coupling due to an improper use of surrogate methods.
source: However, our results show a lack of convincing evidence for n:m phase-locking in the two hippocampal datasets analyzed here, and further suggest that previous work may have spuriously detected phase-phase coupling due to an improper use of surrogate methods, a concern also raised for phase-amplitude coupling (Aru et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis with reference to concerns raised in prior work.

claim: Differences in analyzed epoch length are likely to explain the high variability of Rn:m values across different studies.
source: Based on our results, we believe that differences in analyzed epoch length are likely to explain the high variability of Rn:m values across different studies, from ~0.4 (Zheng et al., 2016) down to 0.02 (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the epoch length dependence demonstrated in the study.

claim: There is currently no convincing evidence for genuine theta-gamma phase-phase coupling using the Rn:m metric when examining LFP epochs of up to 100 s of prominent theta activity.
source: In any case, our work shows that there is currently no convincing evidence for genuine theta-gamma phase-phase coupling using the same phase-locking metric (Rn:m) as employed in previous studies (Belluscio et al., 2012; Zheng and Zhang, 2013; Xu et al., 2013, 2015; Stujenske et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2016), at least when examining LFP epochs of up to 100 s of prominent theta activity.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Gamma is not a clock.
source: In contrast to these models, however, our results show that the theta phases in which gamma cycles begin/end are not fixed across theta cycles, which is to say that gamma cycles are not precisely timed but rather drift; in other words, gamma is not a clock (Burns et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results with reference to prior work.

claim: If theta-gamma neural coding exists, the precise location of gamma memory slots within a theta cycle is not required for such a code.
source: If theta-gamma neural coding exists, our results suggest that the precise location of gamma memory slots within a theta cycle is not required for such a code, and that the ordering of the represented items would be more important than the exact spike timing of the cell assemblies that represent the items (Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the results.

claim: The ordering of represented items would be more important than the exact spike timing of the cell assemblies that represent the items in theta-gamma neural coding.
source: If theta-gamma neural coding exists, our results suggest that the precise location of gamma memory slots within a theta cycle is not required for such a code, and that the ordering of the represented items would be more important than the exact spike timing of the cell assemblies that represent the items (Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the results.

claim: There is currently no technique that can differentiate spurious from true phase-phase coupling.
source: While no current technique can differentiate spurious from true phase-phase coupling, previous findings should be revisited and, whenever suitable, checked against the confounding factors and the more conservative surrogate procedures outlined here.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of methodology.

claim: Seven male Wistar rats (2–3 months; 300–400 g) were used in the study.
source: We used seven male Wistar rats (2–3 months; 300–400 g) from our breeding colony, kept under 12 hr/12 hr dark-light cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Recordings were made from the dorsal hippocampus through either multi-site linear probes or single wires.
source: We recorded from the dorsal hippocampus through either multi-site linear probes (n = 6 animals; 4 probes had 16 4320 μm2 contacts spaced by 100 μm; 1 probe had 16 703 μm2 contacts spaced by 100 μm; 1 probe had 16 177 μm2 contacts spaced by 50 μm; all probes from NeuroNexus) or single wires (n = 1 animal; 50 μm diameter) inserted at AP −3.6 mm and ML 2.5 mm.
evidence: This is a description of the recording methods.

claim: Data from three additional rats were downloaded from the Collaborative Research in Computational Neuroscience data sharing website.
source: We also analyzed data from three additional rats downloaded from the Collaborative Research in Computational Neuroscience data sharing website (www.crcns.org) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). These recordings are a generous contribution by György Buzsáki's laboratory (HC3 dataset, Mizuseki et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This describes an additional dataset used in the study.

claim: Recording sessions were performed in an open field (1 m x 1 m) and lasted 4–5 hr.
source: Recording sessions were performed in an open field (1 m x 1 m) and lasted 4–5 hr.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Raw signals were amplified (200x), filtered between 1 Hz and 7.5 kHz, and digitized at 25 kHz.
source: Raw signals were amplified (200x), filtered between 1 Hz and 7.5 kHz (third order Butterworth filter), and digitized at 25 kHz (RHA2116, IntanTech).
evidence: This describes the signal processing methods.

claim: The LFP was obtained by further filtering between 1–500 Hz and downsampling to 1000 Hz.
source: The LFP was obtained by further filtering between 1–500 Hz and downsampling to 1000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the LFP extraction method.

claim: Active waking and REM sleep periods were identified from spectral content (high theta/delta power ratio) and video recordings.
source: Active waking and REM sleep periods were identified from spectral content (high theta/delta power ratio) and video recordings (movements during active waking; clear sleep posture and preceding slow-wave sleep for REM).
evidence: This describes the behavioral state identification method.

claim: The results were identical for active waking and REM epochs.
source: The results were identical for active waking and REM epochs; throughout this work we only show the latter.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of results across behavioral states.

claim: Band-pass filtering was obtained using a least squares finite impulse response (FIR) filter.
source: Band-pass filtering was obtained using a least squares finite impulse response (FIR) filter by means of the 'eegfilt' function from the EEGLAB Toolbox (Delorme and Makeig, 2004).
evidence: This describes the filtering method used.

claim: The filter order was three times the sampling rate divided by the low cutoff frequency.
source: The filter order was three times the sampling rate divided by the low cutoff frequency.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the filtering method.

claim: To estimate the instantaneous theta phase of actual data, the LFP was filtered between 4–20 Hz.
